summary: BotService implements the documented Connect/Disconnect/Get/TestMessage lifecycle and honors all hardening levers required by the tech-spec: AES-GCM token at rest, SHA-256 webhook secret hash, generic 409 messages, ProjectService.requireOwned as first reactive step on every public method, INCR-every-attempt brute-force counter with DEL-on-success and AppException-aware fail-open, best-effort compensating deleteWebhook on Connect persist failure, and audit metadata that excludes token/IV/ciphertext/secret. One major and three minor findings remain; the major one is a token-in-logs leak vector via WebClient transport-error messages, which is the same R1/AC17 risk the rest of the file goes to great length to avoid.

findings.title: Bot token may leak into WARN logs via raw WebClient error message on Disconnect / Connect rollback
findings.owasp: A09 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures (and A02 Cryptographic Failures by extension — plaintext credential in logs)
findings.cwe: CWE-532 Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File

findings.title: Plaintext token captured into downstream lambda closures during Disconnect (lifetime longer than necessary)
findings.description:
`doDisconnect` declares `String plaintextToken` (line 210), passes it to `telegramApiClient.deleteWebhook(plaintextToken)` (line 212), and the chained `.onErrorResume(err -> ...)` (line 214) and `.flatMap(deleted -> ...)` (line 219) lambdas are constructed in the same enclosing method. Java captures effectively-final locals by reference into lambda objects, so the `plaintextToken` String reference stays reachable on the heap through the lambda objects for the lifetime of the entire reactive subscription — long after the `deleteWebhook` call no longer needs it. The decisions.md / task spec language says plaintext "lives only on the local stack frame"; in practice it lives until the Mono chain is GC-eligible.

The practical risk is small (no logging, no serialization, plaintext is bot-owner-controlled token), but the file's own comment at line 207 ("Plaintext token lives only on this stack frame") overstates the guarantee. Heap dump during an in-flight disconnect would expose the token.
findings.owasp: A02 Cryptographic Failures (extended lifetime of decrypted secret)
findings.recommendation: Two options, in order of cost: (1) Document the actual lifetime in the source comment ("effectively-final closure capture; reachable until the subscription completes") so future readers do not assume stack-only. (2) If you want to shorten lifetime, refactor `doDisconnect` so the Telegram call resolves to a boolean BEFORE the `.flatMap` over the bot update, and pass `plaintextToken` through a fresh `Mono.fromCallable` boundary so the local goes out of scope after the call. The first option is sufficient for this task; the second is a refactor decision out of scope for Task 6.
findings.cwe: CWE-316 Cleartext Storage of Sensitive Information in Memory

findings.title: DuplicateKeyException substring matching is unguarded against an attacker-controlled index name
findings.description: `mapPersistError` does `message.contains("projectId_unique_connected")` and `message.contains("telegramBotId_unique_connected")` as fail-safe discrimination. The index names are platform-fixed (declared in Bot.java) and not attacker-controlled, but the substring check is unbounded: if BOTH substrings appear in a single message (driver edge case or future MongoDB driver change that lists all candidate indexes), the first match wins arbitrarily. The recheck fallback at lines 184-188 already handles the "neither match" case correctly; the "both match" case is theoretical but produces an arbitrary winner without falling back to the authoritative recheck.
findings.owasp: A04 Insecure Design (parsing-driven control flow with weak invariants)
findings.recommendation: Treat "both substrings present" the same way as "neither present" — fall through to the recheck query so the answer is sourced from the authoritative collection state, not from message-substring matching. Equivalently, change the discrimination to short-circuit-then-verify: only return the per-project conflict from the substring branch if the recheck query confirms the platform-wide index is clean. Low priority because the failure mode is a misclassified 409 code (still 409, still no information disclosure, still triggers the same compensating deleteWebhook).

findings.title: tokenSuffix exposes a 3-character suffix of the bot token at rest
findings.description: `tokenSuffix = token.substring(token.length() - 3)` persists the last 3 characters of the bot token plaintext into Mongo (UI display purpose per tech-spec). 3 chars from the `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{30,50}` alphabet is only ~17.8 bits of entropy revealed (log2(64^3) ≈ 18). This is by design and matches the tech-spec / Data Model. Risk acceptance is documented elsewhere; calling out here so the design choice is explicit in the security record: a Mongo backup leak reduces brute-force search space for the remaining 27–47 token characters by 18 bits. Combined with R7 (webhook secret hashed) and R1 (token AES-GCM at rest), this is an acceptable defense-in-depth trade-off but not zero-risk.
findings.owasp: A02 Cryptographic Failures (partial plaintext disclosure of credential)
findings.recommendation: No action required for Task 6 — this is explicitly part of the design (D17 + AC1 require `tokenSuffix` populated for UI display of the masked token). Recorded for completeness so the residual risk is visible in the security log. If ever revisited, consider storing the suffix encrypted under the same key as the full token, or moving to a per-bot ID display label sourced from Telegram username only.
findings.cwe: CWE-200 Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
